posts.title: No, AI Isn't Making Our Fees Go Down
posts.excerpt: Clients keep asking whether using AI means our costs are coming down. The work didn't shrink — here's what actually changed, and what we refuse to hand over.
posts.body:
I wrote recently about where AI belongs in our design process and where it very much doesn't. This one's about the business side, because lately the questions have gotten pointier.

The one I hear most: since you're using AI, surely your costs are coming down?

Big fat no. If anything, there's a decent argument they should go up.

## The work didn't shrink

We're likely spending more time on each project now, not less. What's changed is that the work comes out better and moves faster.

But the actual list hasn't shortened by a single line. Concepts, design, space planning, drawings, drafting, code review, jurisdictional review, pricing review, more drafting, engineering coordination, engineering review, renderings, finish selections, specifications. It goes on. And on.

A different tool doesn't delete any of that. It just means we get through it a little quicker and a little sharper, so projects keep their momentum. Where we might once have told you three months, partly because we're juggling five other things, we can now often say two.

A lot of that comes down to letting AI work while we don't. We'll set renderings running overnight, let things churn while the office is dark, and by morning it's waiting for us. Less about AI being brilliant, more about being clever with the hours.

## Please, don't buy every app

Here's my genuine warning, from someone who has not taken her own advice: don't throw money at every shiny new AI tool that appears. I have been an absolute sucker for this. I've tried an embarrassing number of them. A few were terrific.

But the real value was never in the app. It's in working out how this fits your business, your team, your process, your brain. Everyone needs a different kind of help. Not everyone needs code analysis, or drawing review, or rendering support. There's no one-size-fits-all here, and anyone promising you otherwise is selling something.

## So we're building our own

We're currently building a team app for internal communication, drawing management, and a client portal. There's no shortage of software out there, but none of it did what we needed for the way our team actually works. So we figured, why not?

Will our software work for everyone else? Almost certainly not. And honestly, that's the whole point.

## Where AI has truly earned its seat

The business side is where it shines for us. Running the company, wrangling finances, building internal tools so the team can coordinate properly and actually bring clients and contractors into the fold. As a kind of tireless assistant, it's a joy.

And let's be honest with each other: almost none of us got into design for the math and the spreadsheets. AI's willingness to take that off our plates is unmatched. It sorts purchasing and procurement. It helps us build proposals that are genuinely beautiful. It swallows the tedious things that used to eat an entire evening, and it never once complains.

## Where all this is heading

I'm not going to pretend nothing is changing. Parts of our industry will disappear. That's real, and I think the people digging their heels in are going to find it very hard to move their businesses forward.

So we're pivoting. We're building our own processes and tools so we can keep doing our best work and take on more of it, with AI humming away in the background where it belongs.

But here's what I keep landing on. The more of this becomes automated, the more valuable the human part gets. Taste. Judgment. Knowing when to break a rule. Sitting across from someone and understanding what they actually want, which is rarely the thing they said first. I don't think AI is coming for that. If anything, I think it's about to make it the most valuable thing we sell.

The question was never whether to use AI. It's how to use it well, and what you refuse to hand over.

And yes, same as last time: I wrote every word of this myself, then had AI tidy up my typos. Only fair to say so.

posts.title: What AI Can't See in a Room
posts.excerpt: Yes, we use AI. Happily. But it comes in after the real work is underway — and it will never tell you the truth about what your money will buy.
posts.body:
Quick confession before we dive in: I used AI to help write this post.

Did I have it write the whole thing? Absolutely not. Every word here is mine. I just handed it over at the end to catch my typos and wrangle my run-on sentences, of which there are many. Which, funnily enough, is more or less the entire point I'm about to make.

I've been circling this topic for months. It's a touchy one right now, and I understand why. But I also think it's a little silly to pretend a tool isn't sitting right there on the table.

So, the questions we get constantly: do we use AI? How? Are we nervous about our jobs? Yes, we use it. Happily. But we bring it in after the real work is underway, never before. It's an assist. It's a finishing layer. It is not the thing that makes the thing.

## The part that still belongs to us

Here's what I keep coming back to. Design was never really about pretty pictures. It's about the way someone drifts through their kitchen at six in the morning before anyone else is up. It's where the afternoon light lands in October. It's whether the backpacks get dumped in the entry or the mudroom, and whether anyone will actually walk the extra ten feet to do it. It's a client telling me they want a wide-open kitchen when what they really mean is they'd rather not be watched while they cook.

None of that fits in a prompt. It comes out of a conversation, a walkthrough, a few nosy questions, and an enormous amount of listening. That's the part of this work I'd defend with my whole chest, and it's the part I worry about when someone hands their entire project to a chatbot and calls it done.

And here's the thing I find quietly hopeful: the more polished and automated everything gets, the more people seem to ache for the opposite. The hand-thrown bowl. The imperfect plaster. The room that could only belong to one family. Design is drifting back toward warmth and toward the human fingerprint, and I don't think that's a coincidence. I think we're all a little tired of perfect.

If you're using ChatGPT to dream up your space, please do. It's fun. But talk to a designer too, if it's in your budget. I know it isn't always, and AI genuinely helps people taking on smaller projects. It has a seat at the table. It just isn't going to plan your house around the life you actually live, and it will never look at your existing structure and tell you the truth about what your money will buy.

## The images clients bring me

I get AI images from clients constantly, and honestly? I love it. Someone sends me five renderings and within thirty seconds I understand their taste better than I would after an hour of adjectives. It's a shortcut straight to the feeling, and that's a gift.

The flip side is that when there's no real basis of design underneath it, AI makes everything look more or less the same. Once you notice it, you can't unsee it. The same finishes. The same proportions. The same soft, flattering glow on every surface. It'll tell me whether you lean light or dark, modern or classic, and that's genuinely useful. But it misreads budgets all the time, and it has a real talent for making things far more complicated than they need to be.

So after I've absorbed the feeling, I tend to leave it at the door.

Because the moment we start walking the actual house, the design shifts. I'd say ninety percent of the time it shifts significantly. We talk money. We talk about what's structurally possible inside that number. We talk about what's actually available here, and what it costs here. The image was never a plan. It was a mood. And a mood is a beautiful place to begin and a terrible place to build from.

## A word about renderings

We do run AI over our renderings. It adds a realism clients adore, and it helps people genuinely picture themselves in a room instead of squinting at a gray box.

But we have to get that rendering about ninety percent of the way there first. Otherwise it develops opinions. You'll get strange scale, details nobody asked for, little flourishes invented out of thin air. And here's my favorite quirk: the more times you ask it to revise, the more it quietly redecorates behind your back. A window slides. A cabinet puts on weight. Something you never touched looks subtly, maddeningly different.

So we've learned to push our renderings further along before AI ever lays eyes on them, so it only needs one pass. Give it less room to improvise and it behaves beautifully.

You can usually still tell. It's very good. It is not perfect.

## The apps that promise to price your remodel

There's a whole crop of apps right now promising they'll read your room, price your room, and hand you a tidy estimate. We've tried plenty of them, because of course we have. At thirty thousand feet, there's something there. You'll get a ballpark.

But down in the weeds, where projects actually live and breathe, it comes apart. Every state is different. Every jurisdiction is different. Every contractor is different. No app on earth holds all of that.

We had a client arrive with a number AI had given them, feeling very good about it. What it missed: Washington State energy code, which is not optional and is not cheap. It also didn't realize the cabinets it had designed weren't standard sizes, so they'd have to be custom. And it couldn't possibly know there was HVAC running through the wall, which meant the plumbing had to move.

Their project got dramatically more expensive over the course of one afternoon. That's not a conversation anyone enjoys having.

## Where it's earned its keep on the architecture side

One of the genuinely hardest parts of my job is keeping up with code. In Washington, requirements swing wildly from one jurisdiction to the next, and then you stack state requirements and the International Building Code on top of that. Keeping every change straight is a full-time job nobody's hired for.

So AI has quietly become part of our QC. We run a first pass on drawings before anything goes out to a client or a city, and it's excellent at explaining code sections. That's been a real relief.

But it isn't drawing anything. It doesn't know local conditions beyond what's printed on the page. It can't walk a site and catch the thing you only notice standing in the room with your head tilted. And it certainly can't be the person holding the line between the client, the designer, the engineer, and the city.

I'd genuinely love to see jurisdictions use AI to move through initial plan review faster. But a human has to stay in it, because no two conditions are ever truly the same, and that is precisely the thing AI is worst at noticing.

## So, my honest advice

Take it with a grain of salt. Use it to find your style, to get excited, to finally show someone the thing that's been living in your head. That part is wonderful.

And then bring it to someone who can stand in the room with you. AI is a very good tool. It's at its best when there's a person behind it who knows the house, knows the budget, and knows the people who'll be living there long after the renderings are forgotten.

posts.title: Inside the Miller Residence: One House, Room by Room
posts.excerpt: A West Seattle whole-home project — two-tone cabinetry, brass carried everywhere, and a blue-green thread that ties forty-one photographs into one house.
posts.body:
The Miller Residence in West Seattle is the largest gallery on this site — forty-one photographs, kitchen through laundry room. That's deliberate. A single hero shot tells you what a kitchen looks like; a full set tells you whether a house was designed as one thing or decorated room by room.

Here's what we were thinking as it came together.

## The plan comes before the palette

The kitchen sits at the center of the main floor, open to dining and living, with the view held at the end of the sightline. Everything after that decision — where the island lands, how tall the pantry column runs, which wall gets the range — follows from the way the family actually moves through the floor: in the back door, drop everything, cook, eat, sit down.

We draw that circulation before we choose a single finish. It's the least glamorous part of the process and the part that decides whether the finished house feels effortless.

## Two cabinet finishes, doing two different jobs

The perimeter uppers are painted light, which keeps the ceiling height and the windows doing the work. The base cabinets and the tall column are warm wood, which grounds the room and gives the island something to talk to.

A two-tone kitchen fails when the split is arbitrary. It works when each finish has an assignment — light where you want the room to recede, wood where you want weight.

![Painted uppers keep the perimeter light; the wood base cabinets carry the weight.](assets/img/work/miller/miller-13.jpg)

## One metal, carried all the way through

Brass runs everywhere here: the faucet and pot filler, the cabinet hardware, the pendants over the island, the sconces in the baths, the shower set, the mirror frames.

The rule we use on every project: **pick one dominant metal and commit to it**, then allow a single accent if a room genuinely needs one. Three metals chosen room by room is the fastest way to make a well-built house look unplanned.

## A color that travels

Blue-green shows up at the island stools, on the living room walls, in the secondary bath, and again on the laundry cabinetry. Nobody walking through reads it as a scheme — they just feel that the rooms belong to each other.

That's the whole point of a whole-home palette. It isn't about painting everything one color. It's about repeating two or three notes often enough that the house holds together.

![The same blue-green that shows up at the island stools returns on the living room walls.](assets/img/work/miller/miller-19.jpg)

## Be quiet in some rooms so you can be loud in others

The kitchen backsplash is a calm stone. The guest shower is a lantern-shaped tile. The primary bath floor is a checkerboard. The laundry and mudroom floors are patterned.

Utility rooms are the best places in a house to take a risk. They're small, they're cheap to change, and they're where a little personality goes the furthest.

![Patterned floor tile and painted cabinetry in the laundry room.](assets/img/work/miller/miller-37.jpg)

## Why an architect ends up in your kitchen

Cabinet elevations, lighting layouts, and tile layouts all get drawn before anything is ordered. Not because drawings are fun, but because that's when a misaligned sconce or a pendant that lands three inches off the island centerline is still free to fix.

That's the difference between a designer's eye and a set of construction documents — we bring both, and the second one is what keeps the first one from getting expensive on site.

## See the whole house

The full set is in [Select Work](work.html). Photography by Emily Keeney.

If you're planning something similar — a whole-home remodel where the kitchen, baths, and the rooms in between all have to add up — [tell us about it](contact.html).

posts.title: The Strauss Residence: Traditional Detail, Working Hard
posts.excerpt: A furniture-style island, arches used more than once, and a green-tiled shower — how classic detailing makes a house feel current instead of dated.
posts.body:
Traditional detail has a reputation problem. Done carelessly it reads dated — heavy, fussy, a decade behind. Done with discipline it does something no minimal interior can: it makes a new house feel like it has been there a while.

The Strauss Residence is our argument for the second version.

## The island as a piece of furniture

The perimeter cabinetry is inset, painted, and quiet. The island is not — it's dark wood with turned legs and a stone top, sitting in the room like a table somebody moved in rather than a run of cabinets that happened to stop.

That contrast does real work. It breaks up what would otherwise be an unrelieved wall-to-wall kitchen, and it gives the open plan a center that reads as a room, not a corridor.

![The island sits in the room like a table somebody moved in.](assets/img/work/strauss/strauss-04.jpg)

## One shape, used more than once

There's an arch over the range and an arch at the opening into the dining room. Two instances, same family of curve.

A detail used once is decoration. A detail used two or three times in the same house becomes a language — the eye picks it up on the second appearance and starts reading the plan as intentional.

![The arched opening into the dining room answers the arch over the range.](assets/img/work/strauss/strauss-03.jpg)

## Cabinetry that goes all the way up

Running the cabinets to the ceiling is one of the highest-return moves in a remodel. You gain real storage, you lose the dust ledge, and — most importantly — the wall reads as architecture instead of furniture parked against plaster.

The long brass pulls do the rest, drawing the eye vertically and making a nine-foot wall feel taller than it measures.

## Two metals, two rooms, no confusion

Brass in the kitchen. Polished nickel in the bath.

That isn't inconsistency — it's the mixing-metals rule applied properly: **one dominant metal per room, carried completely**, rather than a little of everything everywhere. Each room reads as decided. Walk between them and you notice warmth in one and coolness in the other, which is exactly the intent.

## Color where nobody expects it

The shower is tiled floor to ceiling in a green glazed tile with enough variation that no two pieces read the same, and the ceiling above it is dark.

A small, enclosed, wet room is the safest place in a house to commit to a color. There's no adjacent furniture to fight, the tile is going in once, and the payoff — the moment someone opens that door — is out of all proportion to the square footage.

![Green glazed tile floor to ceiling, with a dark ceiling above it.](assets/img/work/strauss/strauss-05.jpg)

## Detail that reads from across the room and up close

The stair hall is paneled, with a white-oak rail and treads against white risers. From the entry you register proportion and light. From the third step you register the joinery.

Good detailing has to survive both distances. That's the standard we hold on every set of drawings that leaves the studio.

## See the project

The Strauss Residence is in [Select Work](work.html), alongside the rest of our whole-home projects.

Thinking about a remodel where classic detail has to feel current? [Start a conversation](contact.html).

posts.title: Design With Intent: How We Begin Every Project
posts.excerpt: Great spaces don't start with a mood board — they start with how you actually live. A look inside the questions we ask before a single finish is chosen.
posts.body:
Every project at Drift begins the same way: not with a paint color, but with a conversation about life.

## Function first

Before we shape a single sightline, we map how a space will really be used — where the light lands in the morning, where people gather, where the quiet corners need to be. Only then does the design work begin.

## The details that matter

From the placement of furnishings to the flow between rooms, we design for the way a home is lived in and remembered. The result is a space that feels effortless — dynamic where it should be, calm where it needs to be.

That discipline is what turns a house into a home, and a project into something lasting.

posts.title: Staging That Sells: Why Presentation Moves Markets
posts.excerpt: In today's market, buyers decide in seconds. Here's how elevated, strategic staging helps a listing show its best — and sell faster.
posts.body:
A beautifully staged home doesn't just look better — it *sells* better.

## First impressions are everything

Buyers form an opinion within moments of walking in (or scrolling past a listing photo). Thoughtful staging highlights architecture, warms up empty rooms, and helps buyers picture themselves at home.

## Strategy, not just style

We stage to the market and the buyer — curated furnishings, considered styling, and a flow that photographs beautifully and shows even better in person. It's design in service of the sale.

Ask us about our **Pay-At-Close** option, which lets qualifying sellers defer their staging investment until the home sells.

posts.title: Permit-Ready: Building Faster With Pre-Approved Plans
posts.excerpt: Our library of ready-to-build plans — including The Si Plan, pre-approved in the City of Everett — can shorten your path from idea to groundbreaking.
posts.body:
Building a home is a big undertaking. Starting from an approved plan can make it dramatically simpler.

## What 'Basic Plan' approval means

In the City of Everett, our **Si Plan** is approved as a Basic Plan — cleared to build on an expedited permit with no modifications required. That means less time in review and a faster path to construction.

## A plan for the way you live

Every plan in our library can be built as-drawn or tailored with modifications. We'll walk you through pricing for the plan as-is and for any changes you have in mind.

Browse the library and ask which plans are approved in your jurisdiction.
